structure.title: I
structure.summary: In the spring of 1922, Nick Carraway arrives in West Egg and rents a modest eighty-dollar bungalow, acquiring an old Dodge, a Finnish housekeeper, and a dog that soon runs away; he immerses himself in twelve volumes on banking to become a 'well-rounded man.' Reflecting on his father’s advice to reserve judgment, he recalls how his tolerance made him a confidant in college and later led to disillusionment with the moral chaos of the East, except for Gatsby, whom he uniquely admired for his extraordinary gift for hope. After driving by car to East Egg to visit his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom—whom he knew at Yale—he is introduced to Jordan Baker, who lies motionless on a couch. During dinner at their grand Georgian Colonial mansion, Tom espouses racist views from The Rise of the Coloured Empires, a phone call reveals his affair with a woman in New York, and Daisy confesses her cynical belief that a girl’s best fate is to be a 'beautiful little fool,' followed by a chilling smirk. As Nick returns to his estate, he observes Gatsby standing alone on his lawn, arms outstretched toward a single green light at the end of a distant dock, trembling in the warm summer night before vanishing into the shadows.

structure.title: II
structure.summary: On a summer Sunday afternoon, Nick Carraway travels by train with Tom Buchanan from West Egg to the valley of ashes, where Tom forcibly stops the train to introduce Nick to Myrtle Wilson, wife of the pale and anaemic garage owner George Wilson; they walk under the faded eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg’s billboard to Wilson’s dilapidated garage, where Myrtle immediately asserts dominance over her husband. Tom arranges for Myrtle to meet him on the next train to New York, where she purchases magazines, perfume, cold cream, and an Airedale dog from a street vendor before taking a lavender taxicab to her rented apartment on 158th Street. There, Myrtle changes into a cream chiffon dress and hosts a raucous gathering with her sister Catherine and neighbors Mr. and Mrs. McKee, drinking heavily and performing exaggerated upper-class mannerisms while Nick becomes drunk and reads Simon Called Peter; the party descends into chaos when Myrtle drunkenly shouts Daisy’s name, provoking Tom to violently break her nose, after which women scramble to clean the blood with Town Tattle magazine and Mr. McKee, dazed, suggests lunch to Nick in the elevator; Nick later finds himself alone in the cold, dim lower level of Pennsylvania Station at dawn, exhausted and disoriented, waiting for the four o’clock train.

structure.title: III
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway, Nick, receiving a formal invitation to attend Jay Gatsby’s extravagant party at his Long Island mansion, arriving by car after seven p.m. Amidst lavish details—five crates of weekly fruit deliveries, a machine extracting juice from two hundred oranges, hundreds of feet of canvas and colored lights, and a full orchestra playing in the garden—Nick observes drunken guests spreading rumors about Gatsby’s mysterious past, including claims he killed a man or was a German spy. He encounters a drunken guest in the library who marvels at the authenticity of Gatsby’s real books and later bonds with a war veteran who invites him to ride a hydroplane the next morning, yet still has not met Gatsby. Eventually, Nick sits at a table with a rowdy girl and a man who reveals himself to be Gatsby; they briefly connect over wartime service, and Gatsby invites Nick to ride the hydroplane at nine o’clock. As the party descends into chaos—a chorus girl sings while weeping ink-tears, couples fight, and a new coupé crashes into a wall, leaving one wheel lost—Nick witnesses Owl Eyes claim he wasn’t driving and a dazed man emerge asking for a gas station. Jordan Baker is called away by Gatsby for a private hour-long conversation, and Nick departs as Gatsby stands alone on the porch, formally bidding farewell under a faint moon. Later, Nick reflects on his daily life in New York: working at the Probity Trust, lunching with clerks in dark restaurants, studying investments in the Yale Club’s library while avoiding rioters upstairs, and walking home at night along Madison Avenue to Pennsylvania Station, feeling both drawn to and lonely amid the city’s twilight energy. He reconnects with Jordan Baker in midsummer, initially flattered by her fame as a golf champion, but later discovers her dishonesty through her admission of lying about damaging a borrowed car and cheating in a past tournament; she claims she hates careless people and likes Nick because he isn’t one, yet he remains emotionally bound to a woman back home, to whom he still writes letters signed 'Love, Nick,' concluding with his declaration that he is one of the few honest people he has known.

structure.title: IV
structure.summary: On a Sunday morning, Gatsby’s mansion erupts into chaotic revelry as guests from East Egg, West Egg, and New York arrive by car, including dozens of named figures like the Chester Beckers, Klipspringer, and Ferret, many of whom gossip wildly about his rumored criminal past while unaware of the host’s true identity; later that day, Gatsby picks up Nick Carraway in his cream-colored car with nickel trim and, during a drive to Manhattan, presents an elaborate, fragmented account of his past—including Oxford education, European travels, and wartime honors from Montenegro—backed by a medal and photograph, while subtly hinting at a request involving Jordan Baker; at noon in a cellar on Forty-second Street, Gatsby introduces Nick Carraway to Meyer Wolfshiem, who recounts the murder of Rosy Rosenthal and chillingly admits to fixing the 1919 World Series, before Gatsby abruptly departs and Nick Carraway spots Tom Buchanan across the room only to find Gatsby gone; in a retrospective vignette, Jordan Baker recalls encountering Daisy Fay and Lieutenant Gatsby in Louisville in 1917, followed by Daisy’s emotional collapse on the eve of her wedding to Tom Buchanan after receiving a $350,000 pearl necklace, her marriage, motherhood, and eventual relocation to Chicago; finally, at twilight, Jordan reveals to Nick Carraway that Gatsby bought his mansion solely to be across the bay from Daisy and seeks a quiet tea invitation to reunite with her, prompting Nick Carraway to reflect on longing as he draws Jordan close in a victoria through Central Park.

structure.title: V
structure.summary: On a rainy night, Nick returns to his West Egg home to find Gatsby’s mansion brilliantly lit but eerily silent; Gatsby approaches him nervously, asking Nick to arrange a tea with Daisy without involving Tom. The next morning, Gatsby has Nick’s grass cut and delivers an entire greenhouse of flowers to prepare for Daisy’s arrival. When Daisy arrives in a large open car driven by Ferdie during a downpour, Gatsby is visibly shaken, nearly knocking over a mantelpiece clock, and the reunion is marked by unbearable silence before dissolving into quiet joy. After the rain stops, Gatsby leads Daisy through his opulent mansion—entering through the big postern gate—and shows her empty rooms with Marie Antoinette music-rooms and Restoration Salons, nearly falling down stairs in his dazed wonder. In his study, he throws dozens of expensive shirts—linen, silk, flannel—in vivid colors onto the table, causing Daisy to sob into the fabric, overwhelmed by their beauty. Gatsby then points out the green light at Daisy’s dock, revealing its symbolic meaning has faded now that she is present, and shares photographs of Mr. Dan Cody and his youthful yachting self, which Daisy admires. As rain resumes, Gatsby summons Klipspringer to play piano; the embarrassed lodger performs two songs while Gatsby and Daisy sit in shadowed isolation. Nick observes Gatsby’s return to bewilderment, realizing Daisy cannot fulfill the idealized version of herself he has cherished for five years, and departs alone into the rain, leaving them emotionally absorbed in each other.

structure.title: VI
structure.summary: The chapter opens with a New York reporter arriving at Gatsby’s West Egg mansion seeking a statement, drawn by rumors that Gatsby lives in a moving boat disguised as a house; the narrative then traces Gatsby’s origins as James Gatz of North Dakota, who at seventeen rowed out to Dan Cody’s yacht, the Tuolomee, anchored off Lake Superior, adopted the name Jay Gatsby, and spent five years working aboard in roles including steward, mate, and jailor, internalizing Cody’s refined lifestyle despite being cheated out of a $25,000 inheritance by Ella Kaye after Cody’s death. Weeks later, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s mansion on a Sunday afternoon when Tom Buchanan, Mr. Sloane, and a woman in a brown riding-habit arrive on horseback; Gatsby nervously offers drinks and supper, but their cold detachment and Sloane’s interruption when the woman invites them to join for supper reveal their exclusion of him, leaving Gatsby standing in hat and coat, ready to follow them in his car, as they depart without him. Later, Tom and Daisy attend one of Gatsby’s parties at twilight, where Daisy is visibly unsettled by the raw, unrefined revelry and unfamiliar crowd, while Tom grows suspicious of Gatsby’s background, speculating he is a bootlegger; after the party, Gatsby confides in Nick Carraway his desperate belief that he can repeat the past with Daisy, recalling their first kiss under moonlight five years earlier, when he believed he could ascend to a transcendent state of pure wonder through her.

structure.title: VII
structure.summary: On the hottest day of summer, Nick arrives by train at the Buchanans’ house to find Gatsby waiting, having replaced all original servants with silent, suspicious replacements to avoid gossip as Daisy secretly visits; during a stifling lunch, Daisy openly kisses Gatsby and declares her love, provoking Tom’s suspicion after he reveals his investigation into Gatsby’s past and mocks his Oxford claim. The group departs for New York in two cars—Gatsby driving his yellow car with Nick and Jordan, Tom taking Daisy in his blue coupé—stopping at Wilson’s garage in the Valley of Ashes where a sickly Wilson, now aware of Myrtle’s affair, hesitates to sell gas and offers to sell his old car, while Myrtle watches from the window and mistakes Jordan for Tom’s wife. At the Plaza Hotel, a volatile argument erupts in a stifling suite: Tom exposes Gatsby’s bootlegging ties through Meyer Wolfsheim and pressures Daisy to renounce her past with him; she admits she once loved Tom but now loves Gatsby, yet cannot fully sever her history with Tom, leading Tom to order them to leave together in Gatsby’s car. Later, Myrtle is struck and killed by a speeding car—Michaelis witnesses her shouting before the collision, and though he initially tells police it was light green, a witness identifies it as yellow and traveling 50–60 mph; Tom and Nick arrive at the scene where Wilson, dazed and crying 'Oh, my Ga-od!', is restrained by Tom, who falsely insists his blue coupé is uninvolved. That night, Nick refuses to enter the Buchanans’ house and waits outside, where Gatsby emerges from the shadows to confess Daisy was driving the car that killed Myrtle and vows to take the blame; Nick observes Daisy and Tom quietly sharing food and ale in the kitchen with an air of intimate conspiracy, while Gatsby stands vigil under the moonlight watching the house, alone.

structure.title: VIII
structure.summary: The chapter opens with a sleepless night for Nick Carraway, haunted by a foghorn and disturbing dreams, followed by a dawn rush across Gatsby’s lawn after hearing a taxi arrive, where he finds Gatsby dejected after Daisy briefly appeared at her window before turning off the light. Together, they search the vast, dusty rooms of Gatsby’s mansion for cigarettes, opening French windows to smoke in the dark, as Gatsby recounts his youthful romance with Daisy—how he, penniless and without status, misled her about his background and became irrevocably bound to her idealized image. Later, on the last afternoon before Gatsby’s departure abroad, he and Daisy share a silent, intimate embrace in a warm, fire-lit room, their subtle touches conveying profound connection as Gatsby reflects that his ambitions have faded without her. The narrative then shifts to Gatsby’s post-war confusion: promoted to major after the Argonne battles, he was mistakenly sent to Oxford while Daisy, overwhelmed by her opulent world of orchids, orchestras, and all-night parties, grew emotionally exhausted and turned to Tom Buchanan, whose stability offered her decisive force; a letter informing Gatsby of her decision reached him at Oxford. At dawn on Long Island, Gatsby insists Daisy never loved Tom, blaming Tom’s aggression for distorting her perception, and recalls walking the streets of Louisville after returning from France, revisiting places with her white car, feeling he left her behind as he rode a hot day-coach away. After breakfast, Gatsby reveals he never used his pool all summer; Nick Carraway misses two trains to stay with him, and upon departure, declares Gatsby worth more than 'the whole damn bunch put together,' to which Gatsby responds with a radiant, understanding smile. Meanwhile, in the city, Nick Carraway wakes sweating from sleep, receives a cold, strained call from Jordan Baker who accuses him of unfriendliness, and attempts four times to reach Gatsby’s house but fails because the line is reserved for a long-distance call from Detroit. Elsewhere, George Wilson, consumed by grief over Myrtle’s death and fixated on the yellow car, declares 'He murdered her' after finding a new dog-leash she hid, then stares at the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg and declares 'God sees everything.' After Michaelis leaves him alone, Wilson travels on foot to Port Roosevelt and Gad’s Hill, buys an uneaten sandwich and coffee, vanishes for three hours, and arrives in West Egg, having learned Gatsby’s name and inquired for his house. At two o’clock, Gatsby dons his bathing suit, instructs the butler to deliver calls to him at the pool, retrieves a pneumatic mattress from the garage with the chauffeur’s help, forbids moving the damaged open car, and walks alone toward the pool. The butler waits awake until four a.m. for a call that never comes; the chauffeur later recalls hearing gunshots but does not react. Nick Carraway arrives by car from the station, rushes to the house, and with the chauffeur, butler, and gardener, discovers Gatsby’s body floating on the mattress in the pool, and Wilson’s body nearby in the grass, completing the tragedy.

structure.title: IX
structure.summary: Following Gatsby’s death, Nick Carraway is left to manage the chaotic aftermath at the mansion as police, photographers, and curious onlookers swarm the grounds, while false testimony from Catherine and a detective’s casual label of Wilson as a 'madman' shape a sensationalist media narrative. Desperate to find mourners, Nick Carraway unsuccessfully contacts Daisy—who has vanished with Tom—and receives a cold, evasive letter from Meyer Wolfsheim refusing to attend. The arrival of Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, from Minnesota brings a poignant glimpse into Gatsby’s humble origins through a tattered copy of Hopalong Cassidy containing his childhood self-improvement schedule; only the Lutheran minister, Gatz, Nick Carraway, and servants attend the funeral in a drizzle, where the mysterious man with owl-eyed glasses appears unexpectedly, expresses shock at the sparse turnout, and calls Gatsby 'the poor son-of-a-bitch.' Nick Carraway later confronts Tom Buchanan on Fifth Avenue, who admits he told Wilson Gatsby owned the car that killed Myrtle, justifying it as self-defense while emotionally breaking over a box of dog biscuits left behind; Nick Carraway sees Tom and Daisy as careless people who destroy lives and retreat into wealth. After selling his car and packing his belongings, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s empty house one final time, erases an obscene word scrawled on the steps, and walks to the beach, reflecting on the vanished natural beauty of the island and Gatsby’s futile yet enduring belief in the green light, concluding with the meditation that 'we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.'

plot_summary.plot_summary:
In the spring of 1922, Nick Carraway moves to West Egg, New York, seeking opportunity and self-improvement, renting a modest home next to the extravagant mansion of the mysterious Jay Gatsby. Through his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom—a wealthy, arrogant Yale alumnus—Nick is introduced to the decadent world of Long Island’s elite, including the cynical socialite Jordan Baker. He soon becomes fascinated by Gatsby, whose lavish parties draw crowds of strangers yet conceal the host’s solitary longing: a quiet, obsessive devotion to Daisy, whom Gatsby had loved five years earlier before the war. Nick learns that Gatsby bought his mansion solely to be across the bay from Daisy’s home, and after arranging a tense, emotional reunion between them, Gatsby believes he can recreate the past and reclaim her love.

As Gatsby’s dream intensifies, tensions rise between him and Tom Buchanan, who grows suspicious of Gatsby’s wealth and background. During a sweltering afternoon in Manhattan, Tom exposes Gatsby’s criminal ties through Meyer Wolfsheim and forces Daisy to admit she once loved him but can no longer fully commit to Gatsby. On the drive back, Daisy, driving Gatsby’s yellow car, accidentally kills Myrtle Wilson, Tom’s mistress, in the Valley of Ashes. Tom, knowing Daisy was behind the wheel, manipulates George Wilson—Myrtle’s grief-stricken husband—into believing Gatsby was both her lover and her killer. Meanwhile, Gatsby, in a gesture of devotion, takes the blame for the accident and waits outside Daisy’s house, guarding her from Tom’s wrath. That night, consumed by grief and delusion, Wilson shoots Gatsby in his pool before turning the gun on himself.

In the aftermath, Nick struggles to arrange a proper funeral for Gatsby, but not one of the hundreds who attended his parties shows up; only Gatsby’s father, a few servants, and a mysterious man with owl-eyed glasses attend. Tom Buchanan, unrepentant, confesses to Nick that he told Wilson Gatsby owned the car, justifying it as protection of his own interests. Nick, disillusioned by the moral emptiness of the East, realizes that Gatsby’s dream was noble in its hopefulness, even if tragically misplaced. He reflects on Gatsby’s belief in the green light across the bay—the symbol of an idealized future—and concludes that despite the corruption and carelessness surrounding him, Gatsby represented something rare: an enduring faith in possibility. Nick leaves New York, carrying with him the memory of a man who chased a dream too beautiful to survive the world he sought to win.
